descriptions: The seer is seeing alone; though pure, it sees by conforming to cognitions (YS 2.20).
Unchanging, it always knows the mind's activities (4.18); consciousness does not move into objects (4.22).
Vyāsa: the power of consciousness is unchanging, does not pass over, has objects shown to it, is pure and infinite (YBh 1.2).
Kaivalya: the guṇas, empty of purpose for the puruṣa, return to their source; or the power of consciousness established in its own form (4.34).
Īśvara: a special puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, fruition and residues (1.24), in whom the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed (1.25), teacher of the ancients (1.26), designated by Oṃ (1.27).
negations: not an object (only the seen is object: 4.19)
not the mind, not the buddhi-sattva: 'utterly unmixed' with it (3.35)
not touched by afflictions, karma, fruition or residues (Īśvara, 1.24)
neither the same as buddhi nor wholly different from it (YBh 2.20)
relation_to_self: The puruṣa is one's true self (the seer); taking the instrument of seeing for the seer is I-am-ness (2.6) and taking the non-self for the self is ignorance (2.5).
relation_to_world: The seen (prakṛti: elements and senses, three guṇas) is real, exists for the sake of the seer — for experience and liberation (2.18, 2.21) — and persists for other puruṣas when it has ceased for one who is liberated (2.22).
caveat: Yoga posits many puruṣas (2.22; YBh 2.22), a real prakṛti, and Īśvara as a distinct special puruṣa who is not the material of the world. It does not teach one self of all; a one-truth reading would have to treat this plurality as a standpoint, which Vyāsa and Vācaspati would reject. Vijñānabhikṣu reads Yoga within his Vedānta of non-separation (avibhāga), where souls are non-separate from the Lord — itself a commentator's view. 'Personal or impersonal: both' = the puruṣa is impersonal pure consciousness, Īśvara is personal (a teacher, approached in devotion).
